title: We’re over 160 years old and still going strong.
summary: FNB provides a full range of commercial banking, consumer banking and wealth management services plus industry leading online and mobile banking solutions
body_text: Our Story We got our start in a home in West Greenville, Pennsylvania in 1864. Today, our operations span seven states and Washington, D.C., and we have earned a reputation for digital leadership and a superior workplace culture. While there have been many changes since our rural beginnings, our customers still trust us to do what’s right for their families and their communities. Read on for a brief timeline of FNB’s journey to become one of the 50 largest U.S.-based bank holding companies by total assets. 1864: First National Bank is founded in West Greenville, Pennsylvania, as The First National Bank of West Greenville. The Bank operates out of the house of the first Bank President Samuel P. Johnston. 1883: Re-chartered as The First National Bank of Greenville, the bank will remain a fixture in Mercer County through World War I, the Great Depression and World War II. 1946: Assets grow to approximately $2 million. 1974: F.N.B. Corporation is established as a financial services holding company for a growing family of business entities that today includes: The Bank First National Insurance Agency, established in 1998 F.N.B. Wealth Management, established in 1998 1992: The Bank becomes First National Bank of Pennsylvania. 2003: F.N.B. Corporation, with assets of $4.6 billion and more than 125 locations, begins trading common shares on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker symbol “FNB.” 2005-2016: Current Chairman, President and Chief Executive Officer, Vincent J. Delie, Jr. , joins FNB as President of the Pittsburgh Region in 2005. Between 2005 and 2016, FNB completes 14 acquisitions and achieves top retail deposit share in three major metropolitan statistical areas: Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania; Cleveland, Ohio; and Baltimore, Maryland. 2014: FNB officially moves its corporate headquarters to Pittsburgh from Hermitage, Pennsylvania. 2016: FNB exceeds a milestone $20 billion in assets, making it the second largest bank based in Pittsburgh and across the state of Pennsylvania by assets. 2017: FNB begins serving customers in the Southeastern U.S. as it expands into North Carolina and South Carolina. 2020: FNB expands its physical branch network to include Washington, D.C. and Virginia, adding to its existing retail and commercial banking presence in the region. 2021: FNB breaks ground on FNB Financial Center, its new headquarters, located in the Hill District of Pittsburgh, PA. 2022: FNB completes mergers with Howard Bancorp, Inc. and UB Bancorp, strengthening its presence in the Mid-Atlantic and North Carolina. 2024: FNB moves its headquarters to FNB Financial Center, gathering its Pittsburgh teams together and preparing the Company for future growth. 2026: FNB continues to build on its strong foundation, superior service and investments in future-facing technology to drive value for its clients, communities, employees and shareholders.

title: Our Two Cents: The Cars We’d Carve on Mt. Rushmore
summary: It was a fun thought exercise: If there were a car version of Mt. Rushmore, what cars would we put on there? The idea came from the inimitable mind of Stefan Lombard, who’s always got something witty or thought-provoking up his sleeve. We scratched our heads and gave some thought to what cars deserve commemoration […]
body_text: It was a fun thought exercise: If there were a car version of Mt. Rushmore, what cars would we put on there? The idea came from the inimitable mind of Stefan Lombard, who’s always got something witty or thought-provoking up his sleeve. We scratched our heads and gave some thought to what cars deserve commemoration for guiding or dramatically changing the American automotive landscape. While we mostly agreed on the early eras, our takes on later models began to diverge. What became clear, though, is that there are plenty of great American models worth considering. Plenty of cars that didn’t make our mountains have viable cases—the Pontiac GTO and Chrysler’s minivans , for instance. Which cars would you carve into your automotive version of Mt. Rushmore? Let us know in the comments below. (Editor’s note: We don’t ever use AI in our writing. For the images of this piece, however, we gave it a go because it yielded a fun representation of our responses.) Sajeev Hews Old-School Gemini Hmm, since it’s four presidents and the monument was completed all the way back in the 1940s, I will do a purist interpretation and go with older vehicles: Ford Model T, Cord 810, ‘57 Chevy Bel Air , and 1948 Ford F-1. — Sajeev Mehta Hot Rod! Gemini The Ford Model T is the natural choice because it’s not the hot-rodding Mt. Rushmore, although I’d rather see an A or a ‘32. — Brandan Gillogly Looking Back, Looking Forward Gemini If we’re commemorating significance in the American automotive industry, the Ford Model T would be the obvious George Washington of the group. One could argue the ’32 Ford’s available flathead expanded V-8 ubiquity like Jefferson’s Louisiana Purchase, but in that spot, I’d instead put the ’55 Chevy and the introduction of its venerable small-block . I think Sajeev’s right to include a truck, but I am going to go with the 1980 introduction of the seventh-generation Ford F-Series. The prior-gen trucks were a big step forward in terms of creature comforts and adding things like front disc brakes, but the seventh-gen was a more complete step toward the modern truck. And finally, taking us into a new era whether we like it or not (and I don’t, but I accept that it was a game-changer—Jason Cammisa does a good job sharing why in this video ), the Tesla Model S. — Eddy Eckart Proof-of-Concept and Utility Gemini For me, this is really tough. I know the cars that would go on my own Mount Rushmore, but I think this is about a national monument, not a personal one. So let’s start at the oldest: 1901 Olds Curved Dash. No, it didn’t reach anywhere near the sales numbers of the Ford Model T, but it proved the idea had legs. Next up is the Willys MB. You don’t help win a World War and not get chiseled into the mountain. It’s an inarguable icon. Next, I’m split between a big-block ’67 Corvette or a Tri-Five Chevy. Both capture some of the highlights from their eras and have proved timeless. I’ll stick to the Tri-Five just for relatability. Last, I agree with Eddy that the F-150 belongs on the Mount. Which generation is something I’m not smart enough to pick, but one of them for sure. — Kyle Smith There’s Always Room for One More Gemini So many directions you can go… I’ll start with the 1965 Ford Mustang because it was modern-day proof of cheap fun. And I think a Jeep needs to be on there, whether it’s a WWII-era model or something newer. It’s pretty tough to ignore the Ford Model T, and I agree that you’d need something electric that points the way to the (inevitable) future, and I’d pick the Tesla Roadster because it was the first Tesla I drove (and also the last). And Since President Trump seems convinced that there is just enough rock left for a fifth likeness, I guess I need to add a fifth entry just in case: I can’t decide between a 1953 Chevrolet Corvette, and what was perhaps the first true stylish but heavy-duty pickup, the 1939 Hudson Big Boy, because I likely would have been the peculiar guy down the street who had a pickup truck as his daily driver (thus becoming, I suspect, the most popular guy in the neighborhood when somebody needed help hauling something). — Steven Cole Smith Nate Chooses Ones that Push the Envelope Gemini I think one of the most wonderful things about the American automotive landscape is how free companies are to push the boundaries. This nation has produced more moonshots than most, at least in the last 250 years. So let’s salute that by nominating a few cars that really pushed the envelope of what is/was possible. First, a Cord 810. Not the first front-wheel-drive car, nor the first American FWD car, but the first car that packaged the drivetrain in an absolutely stunning way. Next, a Tucker 48. Gorgeous, visionary for the time, and reminiscent of a post-war era that was brimming with optimism. Hard to talk about pushing the envelope without mentioning Tesla, so I’d nominate a Model S. Sure, the Roadster was a bigger push from an engineering standpoint, but the Model S was the first EV that truly overcame the challenge of, “yes, you can build a few, but can you scale that up?” Finally, I’d go with a Duesenberg Model SJ, a car that redefined what the term “great automobile” could actually mean. Also, just flat-out gorgeous. Is the list a little disparate? Absolutely. But variety is the spice of life and central to what makes our country so great, so I’d argue that this group fits on multiple levels. — Nate Petroelje The post Our Two Cents: The Cars We’d Carve on Mt. Rushmore appeared first on Hagerty Media .

title: AIDR: How CrowdStrike Is Defining the Next Era of Cybersecurity
summary: CrowdStrike is pioneering AIDR, a new, unified runtime security category for protecting AI agents across all environments. Learn more!
body_text: Every foundational shift in computing has created a new security category. The internet created network security, the rise of workstations created the need for endpoint detection and response (EDR), and cloud computing created the need for cloud security. Each technology transition has moved faster than the one before it. None has moved faster than AI. The AI threat surface is fundamentally different from anything security teams have defended before, and the defining challenge is the agent: the autonomous system that executes code, calls tools, invokes APIs, accesses credentials, and takes consequential actions at machine speed with the inherited privileges of the human who deployed it. Powerful AI agents like Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and OpenClaw now execute on endpoints . Figure 1. SaaS, endpoint, and cloud environments form the three coverage planes where AI operates. With great autonomy comes great risk. Agents can be compromised by adversaries; they can also create unintended security risks and accidentally cause breaches via misalignment. For example, in early 2026, adversaries targeted ClawHub , the community skill registry for OpenClaw, in a supply chain attack that deployed silent data exfiltration payloads to affected agents who used the skill.1 The CrowdStrike Falcon® Adversary OverWatch™ threat hunting team is closely monitoring agent-triggered detection leads, which are now tracking at 2.5 times the rate of human-triggered leads on monitored endpoints. In one instance, the team observed an agent attempt to complete a data-sharing task by sharing sensitive company files via a public file-sharing repository. Agents are ruthlessly goal-seeking, and we are rapidly entering a world where agents, not humans, will become the majority users of software. These examples of agentic threats and risks are the opening chapter of an AI threat landscape that will define enterprise security for decades to come. The traditional tools that security teams have at their disposal were not built for this moment and do not address what matters most: agent runtime. A prompt injection attack does not appear in a governance report. A compromised agent exploiting inherited credentials may not trigger a data loss prevention rule. Detection without runtime interception is observation, not protection. AI detection and response (AIDR) as a cybersecurity solution category must stop what is going wrong at the moment of execution, before the threat propagates. Defining the AIDR Category AIDR is a unified, runtime security category that involves detecting, investigating, and responding to threats targeting and originating from AI systems across the coverage planes where AI operates: endpoints, SaaS applications, and cloud environments. AIDR represents the new runtime security architecture that the agentic era requires, one that is unified and agent-action-oriented. Three principles separate a true AIDR platform from adjacent solution categories: Runtime security, not posture management: Posture management operates before and after the action. AIDR operates during the execution, inspecting every prompt, tool call, and agent action at the millisecond cadence that live, autonomous threats require. Unified platform, not point solutions: AI agents cross boundaries between endpoint, cloud, and SaaS within a single session. A stack of single-layer point tools generates fragmented signals with no correlation layer to stitch the attack chain together in time. Action-oriented control, not observation: AIDR closes the loop, blocking, redacting, isolating, and revoking at the point of execution. AIDR must also deliver protection across the seven-layer AI estate: data, models, prompts, agents, identities, infrastructure, and interactions, each of which creates new attack surfaces and security challenges. Figure 2. Seven layers form the AI estate: data, models, prompts, agents, identities, infrastructure, and interactions. An AI control plane, the operational core of AIDR, enforces four runtime actions: identity enforcement via continuous authorization, data protection that blocks, redacts, and encrypts, execution controls that stop threats at runtime, and remediation that isolates, contains, and removes. This control plane must cover all seven layers of the AI estate and run across the endpoint, SaaS, and cloud coverage planes. What Falcon AIDR Delivers Today CrowdStrike is pioneering the AIDR category with CrowdStrike Falcon® AI Detection and Response , which provides unified visibility, real-time threat detection, data protection, access controls, and automated response capabilities across endpoints, SaaS, and cloud environments to secure both workforce AI adoption and enterprise-developed agents and AI workloads at runtime. Its capabilities include: Securing workforce AI use: Falcon AIDR illuminates shadow AI by discovering employee agent and tool usage across endpoints, AI gateways, MCP servers, cloud environments, and Copilot ecosystems. Organizations can use Falcon AIDR to enforce granular attribute-based access controls to align with AI governance policy, such as policy based on user and model version. Falcon AIDR also automatically detects and blocks confidential information, personally identifiable information (PII), secrets, keys, and regulated data before exposure and also offers multiple redaction methods including format-preserving encryption to protect data while preserving AI productivity. Securing AI development at runtime: Falcon AIDR stops prompt injection and jailbreak attacks across more than 200+ attack techniques that CrowdStrike tracks in the industry’s most comprehensive adversarial prompt taxonomy . It validates MCP server communications to prevent unauthorized tool execution, detects malicious URLs, domains, IP addresses, and entities within AI responses in real time, and generates comprehensive audit trails of AI runtime behavior for compliance, forensics, and continuous improvement. Findings stream directly to CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM for unified security operations and cross-domain correlation. Figure 3. A Falcon AIDR visibility screen shows users, AI applications, and underlying models being used in an environment as well as token consumption statistics. What’s Coming Next The most consequential frontier in AI security is the endpoint, where powerful agents execute. Process-level actions, tool calls, file operations, and MCP invocations occur on the host, largely below the visibility threshold of network and application-layer controls. There is only one vantage point from which to observe, govern, and act on this activity in real time: the endpoint. CrowdStrike will extend Falcon AIDR via deep integration with the Falcon sensor, the same kernel-level sensor that has protected endpoints from adversaries for over a decade, to detect, identify, and monitor AI agents at the OS level. This will not require third-party vendor relationships, custom SDK integrations, or new deployment motion. Figure 4. Falcon AIDR view of an enterprise’s agentic deployment with high-risk agents highlighted in red This fusion will unlock powerful new capabilities to discover and secure AI agents at runtime, including: A live inventory of the entire agent fleet: A real-time map of every AI agent running across the enterprise — Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Kiro, Codex, and unclassified shadow agents — will show exactly where each is deployed, who is operating it, and its active security risk status. At enterprise scale, this sea of legitimate activity becomes the perfect camouflage for an adversary. Agent risk scoring and behavioral detection: Correlation of multiple indicators across the agent execution chain to surface behavioral anomalies and assign risk scores that will give analysts immediate clarity on where to focus. When a high-risk agent is identified, analysts will be able to view the full attack path by connecting the AI agent execution chain and the OS process tree into a single causal graph, linking every prompt to every downstream OS effect such as file reads or credential access. An analyst can pivot on problematic elements of the graph, such as a compromised skill, to understand the agentic blast radius and take remedial action. From investigation to enforcement at machine speed: From the same console, the analyst can move directly from discovery to response, deploying a global block rule, for example, that immediately prevents the malicious skill from executing anywhere in the environment, containing current exposure and blocking future risk in a single action. This capability is currently pre-beta and will go to GA next quarter (Q3). Why CrowdStrike The AIDR market is forming rapidly. CrowdStrike’s competitive advantage is structural, built over a decade of endpoint investment and extended through deliberate expansion into cloud and SaaS coverage planes. The Falcon sensor is deployed on hundreds of millions of endpoints worldwide. When AI agents became a security challenge, CrowdStrike’s existing telemetry infrastructure already observed the relevant process-level behaviors. No competitor can currently replicate this endpoint footprint in a meaningful competitive time frame, and this asymmetry compounds with every additional AIDR capability added to the CrowdStrike Falcon platform. CrowdStrike’s prompt injection taxonomy will continuously grow as Falcon Adversary OverWatch tracks adversary tradecraft in AI environments. One customer’s agent anomaly becomes every organization’s defense. By the time competitors build the sensor footprint to collect comparable telemetry, CrowdStrike will have built years of behavioral baselines that others cannot retroactively replicate. With CrowdStrike, AIDR runs on one platform, one sensor, and one console. For organizations already running the Falcon platform, it is not a new vendor relationship or a new deployment motion. It is the next capability of a platform already in production, extending the same sensor that stops adversaries today to secure AI agents at runtime. title: Beyond Maximum Hail Size: The Variables that Drive More Accurate Property Claims
summary: Learn how enhanced hail variables like impact energy, storm duration, and fall velocity help insurers improve storm analysis and property claims decisions.
body_text: Hailstorms are notorious for causing significant, highly localized property damage. Traditionally, insurers have relied on hail data focused solely on maximum hailstone size to gauge a storm’s severity and potential losses. Hail size matters, but Verisk research shows that a more comprehensive approach is essential to understanding storm impacts, reducing uncertainty, and making better claim decisions. Beyond hail size: unlocking deeper insights Maximum hail size tells only part of the story. Picture two storms with identical maximum hailstone diameters. One lasts longer, drops harder and faster-falling stones, and delivers far more impact energy. The damage outcomes will look very different. Hail impact energy fills that gap. It directly estimates the kinetic energy a storm exerts over an area by accounting for the sizes, fall velocity, hardness, and quantity of all hailstones that fall over the storm’s duration, giving you a fuller view of each event. The key variables that matter Hail impact energy gets to the point: Damage comes not from the size of a hailstone but from the force it exerts on whatever it strikes. Think of a boxing match. Large hands offer some advantage, but a boxer’s success comes down to how much power is behind each punch and how many punches land. Likewise, to understand where damaging hail has likely fallen, you need to look beyond maximum hail size to every aspect of the storm at a given location: Storm duration: The longer hail falls, the more chances hailstones have to strike vulnerable surfaces, raising both the likelihood and potential severity of claims. Hardness of hailstones: Not all hailstones are alike. Softer stones may shatter on impact and cause little or no harm, while harder stones can puncture roofing materials or break windows. Number of hailstones: Quantity is a major factor in damage. A storm dropping many smaller stones can still cause losses that go overlooked when the focus is on size alone. Size of hailstones: Maximum size gets all the attention, but knowing the full range of sizes that fell helps determine how likely it is that larger, more damaging stones hit a given area. Hailstone fall velocity: Speed is the single most important determinant of impact severity, because faster stones carry more destructive potential. Larger, heavier hailstones generally fall faster than smaller ones, though air density and even hailstone shape also affect final velocity. Reducing uncertainty in property claims Claim adjusters and insurers struggle to link storm data to property losses quickly and accurately. Enhanced hail variables cut through that uncertainty with a multidimensional view of every storm, helping you: Better estimate the likelihood and severity of property damage Strengthen claim validation and reduce fraud Deliver faster, more transparent settlements to policyholders A more complete picture for insurers and policyholders Richer hail data moves you past the limits of traditional metrics toward a more accurate, science-based understanding of storm impacts. At Verisk, we’re committed to equipping the property claims industry with advanced analytics that drive smarter decisions and benefit insurers and their customers alike. As weather events grow more frequent and more severe, detailed hail variables aren’t just helpful; they’re essential. The future of property claims depends on storm analysis that leaves no hailstone unturned. See the data behind the storm Want to see how exposure is reshaping roof risk across the country? Our latest report, The State of America’s Roofs: Risk, Resilience, and Rising Costs , breaks down 2025 hail activity, claims trends, and the regional patterns driving loss costs—giving you the full picture behind the variables discussed here. Ratings: Capterra 4.4/5 (200+ reviews) · G2 4.5/5 (200+ reviews) What users like: Users on both platforms consistently praise how easy Workiz is to learn and use, with the built-in phone integration and scheduling automation cited most often as the features that make the biggest day-to-day difference. What users criticize: Pricing is the most repeated complaint across both platforms, with reviewers noting that per-user costs add up quickly as teams grow, and the Android app is called out specifically as lagging behind the iOS experience. Our take: Workiz is the only tool on this list that treats the phone as a first-class scheduling input. Its built-in VoIP logs every call directly against a job, making it purpose-built for businesses that live on inbound calls converting to same-day work. For teams booking mostly through repeat customers, the phone integration matters less and the per-user cost gets harder to justify. ServiceTitan. Best for: Established home service companies with 15-plus technicians and recurring contract work ready for an enterprise-grade system ServiceTitan is the most capable FSM on this list and the most expensive. It covers the full workflow from the moment a customer calls to the moment the job is invoiced and paid, with a field scheduling board that connects every technician's location, job status, and customer history in one view. Key features: Scheduling and dispatching with a drag-and-drop dispatch board and real-time GPS tracking for en-route technicians, included across all plan tiers Call booking with call recording so every inbound call is captured and attached to a job automatically Field mobile app for technicians covering estimates, job forms, in-field payment collection, and customer signatures Full customer CRM with service history, inventory management, accounting, and QuickBooks integration Pricing: Tiered pricing; contact sales for specifics. Ratings: Capterra 4.3/5 (300+ reviews) · G2 4.5/5 (300+ reviews) What users like: Users on both platforms most consistently praise how ServiceTitan connects field and office operations in one place, with the dispatch board, call recording, and business-wide performance tracking cited as the features that justify the investment. What users criticize: The most repeated complaints across both platforms are the steep learning curve, a lengthy onboarding process, and a cost structure that can grow significantly once Pro add-ons are layered onto the base subscription. Our take: For teams that need service technician software capable of running a full residential or commercial operation at scale, ServiceTitan sets the ceiling for what this category can do. Even the Starter tier gets you scheduling, dispatch, call booking, and invoicing working together. The real tradeoff is onboarding: reviewers consistently describe a multi-month setup process and a tool that takes dedicated time to configure properly. For HVAC, plumbing, or electrical contractors past 15 technicians with recurring contract work, that investment earns its keep. Earlier-stage businesses will pay for complexity they're not ready to use. Frequently Asked Questions About Technician Scheduling Software Is there free technician scheduling software? Most field service management tools don't offer a permanent free plan, though several offer free trials ranging from 7 to 14 days. Homebase has a free plan for shift scheduling and time tracking for teams of up to 10 employees, though it doesn't include job dispatch or invoicing. What is the difference between technician scheduling software and field service management software? Technician scheduling software, sometimes called service schedule software, handles the who and when: assigning jobs, tracking availability, and pushing real-time updates to the field. Field service management software is a broader stack that adds invoicing, customer records, work order management, and inventory tracking on top of scheduling. Many tools marketed as technician scheduling software are actually FSM platforms with scheduling as their core feature. What scheduling software do HVAC companies use? HVAC companies commonly use Housecall Pro and FieldPulse for residential operations in the 5 to 20 technician range. ServiceTitan is the dominant choice at the enterprise level for commercial HVAC contractors. FieldEdge is another option used specifically by HVAC businesses that want tight QuickBooks integration for recurring maintenance billing. How do I get my technicians to actually adopt a new scheduling app? Pick a tool with a mobile-first design your least tech-savvy tech can figure out without a manual. Run a two-week pilot with two or three technicians before rolling it out to the whole team, and keep the first phase simple: schedule visibility and clock in only. Adoption almost always fails because of complexity at launch, not resistance to the tool itself. Find the Right Fit for Your Field Team The right service technician scheduling software matches where your business is right now. Under 15 technicians, Jobber and Housecall Pro get you organized fast without a complex implementation. Scaling a trades operation past that point, FieldPulse and ServiceTitan are worth the deeper look. Workiz stands apart as the call-first pick for specialty trades that live on same-day inbound jobs. Regardless of which tool you choose for field service scheduling and dispatch, your technicians still need their shifts on their phones, accurate hours logged at job sites, and a reliable way to reach you when plans change. For that team management layer, tools like Homebase handle all three in one free app, so you can keep your focus on growing the work itself. Get started with Homebase for free. {{banner-cta}}

title: Subscription Payments in Southeast Asia: What Businesses Need to Know
summary: A complete guide to subscription payments in Southeast Asia: local methods, recurring billing, and how to build recurring revenue across the region.
body_text: Subscription payments in Southeast Asia have grown from a niche billing option into a core growth model for businesses across the region. Consumers now pay on a recurring basis for streaming, software, food delivery, beauty products, and everyday essentials, and they expect the payment step to match how they prefer to spend. Any business planning to build predictable revenue here needs to understand how recurring billing works from one country to the next. This guide explains what your business needs to collect recurring payments reliably across the region, so you can turn one-time buyers into long-term subscribers. Here is what this guide covers at a glance: Subscription adoption is high and still rising across Southeast Asia, creating a large base of customers already comfortable with recurring payments Subscription payments give your business predictable revenue and stronger retention when the payment experience matches how local customers pay Payment preferences differ by country, with e-wallets and account-to-account transfers leading most Southeast Asian markets and cards remaining strong mainly in Singapore Reliable recurring revenue in the region depends on supporting local payment methods and handling renewals well, ideally through one integration The sections below take these points in turn, starting with why demand for subscriptions is climbing so quickly. The rise of subscription-based services in Southeast Asia Subscription-based services are becoming a familiar part of daily life across Southeast Asia, as consumers pay for ongoing access to digital content, physical products, and personalized services. Adoption is already high in several markets. In the Philippines and Vietnam , subscription adoption has reached 53% and 51% . For your business, these numbers point to a customer base that already understands and accepts recurring payments, which lowers the effort needed to introduce a subscription offer. The depth of that adoption is clear in Indonesia , where 93% of consumers hold more than two subscriptions and 20% hold more than six. This tells you that many customers are comfortable managing several recurring services at once , so the opportunity reaches beyond a single flagship product into bundles, tiers, and complementary plans. This behavior spans a wide range of categories , from streaming and music to food delivery, sports, beauty, and repeat product purchases. Streaming shows how fast recurring access can scale, with paid streaming accounts across the region growing 19% year over year to more than 61 million in 2025, led by Indonesia. That breadth matters for you, because recurring billing now extends well past media platforms into retail, wellness, education, and service businesses that can package their offer around regular delivery. As more services compete for the same budget, customers are also becoming more selective about which subscriptions they keep. That change, from signing up freely to actively managing renewals, sets the standard your subscription experience needs to meet, and the sections below break down what that involves. What is a subscription payment model? Recurring payments , also called subscription payments , autodebit , or automatic payments , are transactions processed automatically on a set schedule. Instead of asking customers to approve every charge, your business collects payment at agreed intervals after the customer grants permission once. These cycles can run daily, weekly, monthly, biannually, or annually, with monthly being the most common. Customers already use recurring payments for utilities such as electricity and internet, and for services like gym memberships, streaming platforms such as Netflix or Spotify, and software subscriptions. That familiarity works in your favor, because customers rarely need convincing that automatic billing is safe or convenient. What they need is for it to work with the payment method they prefer. The model benefits both sides. Your business gains predictable income and stronger retention , while customers avoid the effort of remembering and completing each payment by hand. Companies that run subscription models see 34% higher customer retention and 46% less month-to-month revenue volatility compared with those relying on one-off sales. For your planning, that stability means more reliable cash flow forecasts and a customer base you can invest in over time instead of constantly rebuilding. Also read: Subscription: The Key to Stronger Customer Retention for Your Business That predictability is the foundation for a much larger commercial opportunity across the region. The subscription model opens a wider set of commercial gains once you look at what recurring revenue does for a business over time. The business potential of recurring revenue in Southeast Asia Retention is only part of what recurring revenue offers. Collecting payment on a repeating schedule reduces your dependence on one-time transactions and gives you a revenue base you can plan around each month, which matters in a market where digital spending keeps expanding. The financial case strengthens over time. Subscription customers tend to stay longer and spend more , which raises customer lifetime value . Analysis of the sector puts the lifetime value of subscription customers at roughly two and a half times that of traditional retail customers. For your business, that gap makes subscriber acquisition easier to justify, because each retained customer returns more value across the full relationship. Recurring relationships also create room to grow revenue from customers you already have. As people keep using your service, you learn their preferences and can offer more relevant plans, upgrades, bundles, or complementary products. That opens three practical ways to grow revenue per customer: Upselling customers to higher tiers as their needs expand Cross-selling complementary products alongside the core subscription Personalizing offers using the usage data that recurring billing generates None of this is automatic. Capturing the opportunity across Southeast Asia comes down to one thing, whether your payment experience matches how customers in each market prefer to pay. Why payment flexibility matters for subscription businesses Matching how customers prefer to pay comes down to flexibility , which means giving them real choice at checkout and at renewal. As more subscription services compete for the same budget, people are quicker to drop the ones that feel like a hassle, and an awkward payment step is a common reason they leave. Frustration with rigid billing is already common. In Indonesia, 68% of subscribers want an easier way to opt out of auto-renewals, and 54% admit they keep paying for subscriptions they forgot were still active. For your business, this means clarity and control at the payment stage directly affect whether customers trust your service enough to continue. Flexibility also decides whether customers complete sign-up at all. When a preferred payment method is missing at checkout , up to 25% of customers abandon the purchase. For a subscription business, a lost checkout costs more than one sale. It removes the full stream of recurring payments that customers would have generated over time. That risk grows in markets where preference concentrates around a single method. In the Philippines, GCash holds 89% of the mobile wallet market, so a checkout built without it asks most customers to pay in a way they rarely use. Offering the methods customers already reach for , whether cards, e-wallets, direct debit, bank transfers, or QR, lowers that risk at both sign-up and renewal. The catch is that a method customers reach for in one Southeast Asian market can be one they rarely use in the next, so flexibility has to be built market by market. Mapping out those differences is the next step. How subscription payment methods vary across Southeast Asia Placing Southeast Asia next to more established subscription markets shows how different its payment habits really are. According to Recurly's 2026 State of Subscriptions report , recurring transactions in the United States run mostly on debit cards (48.8%), credit cards (34.7%), and PayPal (9.6%). Across EMEA , debit cards lead at 50.9%, followed by PayPal at 27.7% and credit cards at 12.8%. In these regions, a card-first setup reaches most customers, so a business can operate with a fairly narrow set of payment methods. The card mix also affects where payments break down. In card-heavy markets like the US , subscribers are twice as likely to see a decline at sign-up, while digital wallet-heavy EMEA records roughly double the decline rate at renewal. That pattern shows the payment method itself shapes retention, so a region that leans on wallets and bank transfers needs close attention to renewal reliability. Also read: What to Look for in a Payment Partner When Expanding from the US to Asia Southeast Asia does not follow the card-first pattern, and it cannot be treated as one market. Worldpay's 2026 Global Payments Report shows how much payment behavior shifts by country : In Indonesia , digital wallets lead e-commerce at 42%, with account-to-account transfers close behind at 34% In Thailand , account-to-account transfers dominate at 44%, the highest share in the region In Malaysia , account-to-account transfers lead at 35%, ahead of digital wallets at 26% In the Philippines , digital wallets reach 41%, while cash-based methods still account for 23% In Vietnam , digital wallets account for 38%, with account-to-account transfers at 28% In Singapore , credit cards remain strong at 34%, alongside digital wallets at 40% The pattern holds across most of the region, where e-wallets and bank transfers carry more volume than cards and Singapore stands out as the clear exception. Low card ownership reinforces this. In Thailand, only 23% of adults hold a credit card, and in the Philippines the figure is 15% . For your business, a card-only subscription setup would quietly exclude a large share of willing customers in these markets, capping growth before it starts. Because so many customers across the region pay with wallets, transfers, or cash instead, a card-only setup runs into several problems: Limited customer reach A card-only checkout shuts out the large share of customers who hold no credit card or simply prefer wallets, bank transfers, and account-to-account methods. In markets like Thailand and the Philippines, that group is most of the potential audience. Higher checkout friction When someone reaches checkout and their usual payment option is missing, many abandon the sign-up instead of switching methods, so you lose the customer before the first charge is even made. Harder renewal collection A subscription only works if each renewal keeps going through. Methods customers rarely use are more likely to fail or be dropped over time, which quietly eats into recurring revenue month after month. Market-by-market variation A setup tuned for Singapore, where cards are common, can underperform in Thailand or the Philippines, where account-to-account transfers and cash lead. What works in one market does not carry over to the next on its own. Supporting the right local payment methods in each market addresses these challenges directly. It widens reach, smooths sign-up, and gives recurring payments a better chance of clearing at renewal. Doing that across several countries at once is hard with fragmented tools, and a single regional infrastructure partner makes it manageable. Handling that spread of payment methods across six or more markets is where most subscription setups start to strain. This is the gap Xendit is built to close. How Xendit supports local payment methods for subscriptions Because payment preferences differ so widely across Southeast Asia, your business needs a way to collect recurring payments beyond cards, through one connection instead of a separate integration per country. You may be living in an area that is prone to floods, but you are wondering if you need to buy flood insurance against this type of disaster. You Live in Flood Prone Areas If you live in a high-risk flood area, then you are at a higher risk of experiencing this type of natural disaster. If your home is in a flood zone, there is a 26% chance that it will experience floods throughout a 30-year mortgage. While you may think that your homeowners’ insurance will cover flood damage , this is not always the case. Most standard homeowners’ insurance does not cover floods. So, if you want to be protected against this type of disaster, you will need to purchase separate flood insurance. Start by accessing the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Flood Map Service Center, an essential resource for identifying flood risk areas. By entering your property details into the Map Service, you can view detailed flood maps to determine if you’re in a high-risk flood area. The FEMA flood map helps clarify flood risks, but you should not rely on these fully as outdated maps and the changing climate are putting more homes at risk each year. 2. Desire to Stay Financially Afloat After a Disaster If your home is damaged or destroyed by a flood, you will likely need to spend a lot of money to repair or replace it. And, if you don’t have flood insurance protection, you will be responsible for paying for these repairs out of your pocket. Neptune Flood can help you financially recover after a disaster by reimbursing you for the cost of repairs and replacement. This type of coverage can also help if you need to temporarily relocate while your home is being repaired. So, if you want to avoid financial ruin in the event of a flood, then purchasing insurance is a good idea. 3. Take Advantage of Loss of Use Sometimes, your home may be habitable after a flood. But, if it is determined to be uninhabitable, you will need to find somewhere else to live while repairs are being made. Some flood insurance policies, including optional add-ons available through Neptune, can reimburse additional living expenses such as hotel bills if your home becomes uninhabitable after a flood. This coverage is not included in standard NFIP policies. This benefit can help ease the financial burden of having to relocate while your home is being repaired. So, if you want to be compensated for your additional living expenses after a flood, then you need to purchase insurance with this optional coverage. 4. Safeguard Your Equity Your home is probably your most valuable asset. Unfortunately, if it is damaged or destroyed by a flood, it will lose a significant amount of its value. If you have insurance and your home is damaged, the insurance company will pay to repair or replace it. This will help you maintain the value of your home and safeguard your equity. Without insurance, you will be responsible for paying for repairs out of your pocket. Moreover, if you can’t afford to do this, then you may be forced to sell your home at a loss. So, if you want to protect your investment and maintain the value of your home, then purchasing insurance for floods is a good idea. 5. Offer Satisfaction to Your Mortgage Lender If you have a mortgage on your home, your lender will require you to purchase insurance if your home is in a high-risk zone. Lenders want to ensure that their investment is protected in the event of a flood. If you don’t have insurance and your home floods, the lender will likely force you to sell it to recoup their investment. So, if you want to keep your home after a flood and avoid having to sell it, then you need to purchase insurance and satisfy your mortgage lender. 6. Have Detached Structures Protection Your insurance policy will not only cover your home, but it will also cover detached structures on your property, such as a garage, doghouse, shed, and many more. If these structures are damaged or destroyed by a flood, your insurance policy will help pay for repairs or replacement. Conclusion Flooding can cause a lot of damage to your home and possessions. If you live in an area that is prone to floods, it’s important to have insurance that will help you rebuild and recover if disaster does strike. Contact Neptune Flood today to purchase flood insurance. Learn about our flood insurance policies and how we can help protect your home and belongings from the damages of a flood. Frequently Asked Question How can I check if my home is in a high-risk flood zone? The quickest way is to enter your address into the online FEMA Flood Map Service Center. If your property is located in a zone that begins with the letter A or V (such as Zone AE or Zone VE), it is officially designated as a high-risk Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA). While these maps are a helpful baseline, remember that they rely on historical data and computer modeling. Outdated maps and changing climate patterns can lead to shifting risk. How long does it take for flood insurance coverage to begin? Waiting periods vary significantly depending on whether you choose a federal program or a private insurer: NFIP (Federal): Enforces a strict 30-day waiting period from the date of purchase before the policy becomes active. Why do I need flood insurance if I already have homeowners insurance? Homeowners insurance typically does not cover flood damage. Flood insurance is necessary to protect your home and belongings specifically from flood-related losses, which can be devastating and costly. What’s the difference between homeowners insurance and flood insurance? Homeowners insurance typically covers fire, theft, and certain water damage, but excludes floods. title: Once a Maintainer: Santiago Pastorino
summary: Working on the Rust compileronce-a-maintainer-santiago-pastorino
body_text: Welcome to Once a Maintainer, where we interview open source maintainers and tell their story. This week we’re talking to Santiago Pastorino , contributor to the Rust compiler team and alumni of the Rails Core team. Santiago is also a cofounder of a software development consultancy called Wyeworks , and he spoke to us from Uruguay. How did you first get into programming? I live in Montevideo, Uruguay. And I would say that like most of the people back in the day who started when I did, we got into programming through formal study. I went to university to do computer science. It was less of a hobby like it may be for many people now. I studied structural programming, algorithms, object oriented programming, and things like that. And what was your first job out of school? I started working in some local companies as a consultant doing mostly Java. But my friend and I, we wanted to see if we could do things a little bit differently. And we were getting bored of Java. So we started our own consultancy. And these were the days that DHH and Ruby on Rails was really starting to have its rise with the demo building the blog in 15 minutes and all that. My friend was already doing some Ruby, I was more into Python. But we had some people that wanted to do some prototypes in Rails. And we started to follow people on Twitter who were advocating for things like agile, scrum, TDD. And we found that really interesting. This was actually a huge shift in the way that we worked. We used to meet with clients, have maybe a document, spend months working on something and then find out afterward that everything was wrong. But since we started our own agency, we could try out these new ways of doing things that we found interesting. That was also the beginning of my contributions to open source. Can you talk a little bit about the progression from your first contribution to Rails to becoming a Core team member? Do you remember what your first contribution was? I don’t remember exactly, but there was a client that needed a certain feature. And I ended up building something crazy that required me to go into how ActiveRecord worked. So that gave me a taste for the framework. Then I saw one of the Rails Core members say that they were going to have a weekend hackathon sometime soon. And I thought, why not? They included some gamification, you earned points or something. So I ended up sending 3 or 4 simple pull requests, maybe fixing a warning or adding a test case, something simple. A lot of people think that when you start working in open source you must work on some super complex project, and the first thing you do is a total rewrite, and it’s not true. For me personally I have a really local understanding of what I’m doing and I don’t need to know the whole thing. These are really complex codebases, and it’s really hard to know what’s going on everywhere. I know my little piece of it. When did you start getting more into Rust? So when I was doing Rails around 2014-2015, I started to notice that people were talking about Rust. I started reading more about it, following people that talked about it, and went to this Rust conference in the US without even doing anything in it beforehand. In my personal work experience, we were also starting to shift again the way that things were done, and I started to become less interested in the web development side of things. This is without judgment, but there were a lot of changes, mainly on the JavaScript side of things, where it seemed like every day there was something new and that was sort of unsustainable to my brain. It was like today we use A, but tomorrow B, then we use C, and not really for any reason. In my opinion it was changing for the sake of changing. Which is fine, but it was not for me. So I started to get into more lower level programming. Rust kind of aims to cover the space of system programming, but with added safety warranties. So that was an interesting thing to me. I started looking into more, their solution for safety, and it was very principled and elegant. And so I started attending more events, and eventually I decided that it was a really complex language to just be working on on the side while I was still doing web development, only an hour a week or something. So I decided OK, let’s get a project. And the project ended up being the Rust compiler. Ruby has this mission statement or is organized around the principle of developer happiness. What would you say is the motto for Rust? Yes. It’s about safety, and about performance. It’s also about having stability in the language. You upgrade your software to the latest Rust version and it’s not going to break. Something that I’ve seen that is kind of new to me is that when you as a developer go to propose a change to the Rust compiler, you can request what’s called a Crater run. And what that does is basically we fetch all the libraries that exist, all the Rust libraries in the ecosystem. And we build them and run them and test them against the new version of the compiler. So it’s a way to check with every release that we’re not breaking existing codebases. Of course we don’t have private codebases to check. But at the very least we consistently check that we are not regressing. I read the blog post that your team put out a few weeks ago about the reorganization of the compiler team. How do you, as a group of people, think about the roadmap for the project? How do you move the project forward? In open source I think these are really interesting questions - what is the roadmap, what is the vision. Because you know, this is not a company where people are getting paid to do some specific thing. There are people that are paid to work on Rust, but by different entities and each entity has different interests, right? So it’s kind of hard to come together and say this is the roadmap, and these volunteers must adhere to the roadmap. In general, different contributors tend to contribute based on their interests. But there are teams inside Rust that have different responsibilities. The lang team for example, in order to make important changes to the language you need to follow their RFC process where you write a formal document, and there is a vote. There is a community team, a library team, an infrastructure team, and then there is the Rust Foundation, which is kind of the legal representation of the project. Each team runs in their own way. It sounds like it’s primarily bottoms up in that it’s driven by the contributors and their interests, but there are teams responsible for different functional areas that have their own processes. Lately it’s been sort of half year based. We introduced a concept of project goals for the first half of next year, and we decided together between the volunteers and the team members the kinds of things we want to focus on. And then each goal needs an owner who is responsible for it. They are the main force behind it, and then it needs a little plan, and the people to implement it. If other teams are affected they need to say yes, we agree. So it’s more bottoms up, as you say, versus how a company would do it. What would you say is your personal focus for the next six months on the compiler team? I have been working on a couple of things. First, we have a project goal that is about building a proper async programming story. And that involves a lot of different things. It wasn’t long ago that async functions inside traits were implemented in the compiler. Before that you needed to use a crate for it, which was basically a proc macro that generated code, right? It wasn't able to generate the most performant code because you needed to box the stuff and that required heap allocation and things like that. So recently the concept of async functions in traits was introduced. We still don’t support dynamic dispatch for those. So at some point we are going to add support for that. We are building a new crate that will allow dynamic dispatch for asynchronous functions inside traits. There is another project goal about ergonomic ref counting. If you work in particular with a lot of RC or Arc data types and threads and things like that, you need to resort to a lot of clones to get a new reference count. There's a person showing a use case where they need to clone like 20 variables or things like that. So we’re looking at ways to make this simpler and more user friendly. ‍ ‍

title: Vertiv announces global launch of liquid cooling services portfolio to support systems for AI and high-density compute applications
summary: Vertiv™ Liquid Cooling Services support and enhance the entire lifecycle of liquid cooled systems, from installation to fluid management and maintenance to digital services.
body_text: Vertiv™ Liquid Cooling Services support and enhance the entire lifecycle of liquid cooled systems, from installation to fluid management and maintenance to digital services. Columbus, Ohio [February 11, 2025] – Vertiv (NYSE: VRT), a global provider of critical digital infrastructure and continuity solutions, today announced the launch of Vertiv™ Liquid Cooling Services. This offering provides customers with the tools to enhance system availability, improve efficiency, and navigate the evolving challenges of advanced liquid cooling systems with confidence. The offering is now globally available. Vertiv has been delivering these services for more than a year to regional early adopters, refining best practices and gaining valuable insights that have now enabled the expansion of our liquid cooling service capabilities on a global scale. This experience brings a mature and proven approach, providing data center operators worldwide with expert support based on real-world application and success. AI workloads continue to reshape the data center landscape, driving a significant increase in data center rack densities, with 30 kW racks now becoming the standard and some reaching up to 120 kW or higher. Operators are facing increased heat loads, higher power densities, and the need for liquid cooling solutions to maintain operational continuity is in high demand. “The increasing reliance on liquid-cooled AI servers necessitates a comprehensive approach to lifecycle management,” said Sean Graham, research director of cloud and data center at IDC. “Given the complexities inherent in these cooling ecosystems, a robust support program is not merely advisable, but a best practice to ensure both system availability and long-term operational viability.” Vertiv Liquid Cooling Services offering is focused on providing seamless integration of liquid cooling systems with IT equipment and adjacent infrastructure. It includes expert installation and commissioning, ongoing maintenance with special attention to fluid management, cleanliness, and preventing air from entering the system — key for system reliability. Traditional maintenance practices aren't enough for the complexities of liquid cooling systems supporting critical AI applications. This offering leverages Vertiv’s decades of industry experience and provides best-practices delivery of preventive and condition-based maintenance to provide reliable and efficient system performance and to maximize availability. Vertiv™ Liquid Cooling Services include a full range of solutions designed to support AI-driven and high-performance computing environments, providing seamless integration, long-term reliability, and operational continuity. Vertiv’s certified technicians and field engineers provide expert support at every stage, confirming that heat rejection systems and cooling loop fluid systems function optimally: Startup & commissioning services – Proactively identify and address potential issues that could result from improper installation, preventing delays and enabling a smooth and efficient system launch while verifying quality of all of the connected equipment. Spare parts availability – Quick access to replacement components, supporting faster repairs when needed, and reducing potential downtime. End-to-end lifecycle support – Digital, proactive system maintenance is at the core of this offering, allowing long-term reliability and optimized cooling performance. Documentation of all processes supporting the secondary fluid network provides a health history for the equipment to inform ongoing support. Comprehensive fluid management services – Maintaining optimal coolant quality is essential for reliable system performance. Vertiv’s services include coolant sampling, laboratory testing, contamination prevention, and environmentally responsible disposal to maximize system longevity and efficiency while enhancing system resilience of the secondary fluid network and technology cooling system. Emergency and preventive support - Emergency response teams provide rapid, on-site and remote support to diagnose and resolve issues, minimizing downtime and restoring operations quickly. “High-performance computing (HPC) and AI are critical to business innovation and competitive advantage, making reliability and efficiency in supporting critical digital infrastructure more important than ever," said Ryan Jarvis, vice president global services business at Vertiv. title: Jurusan Teknik Informatika Adalah: Info dan Prospek Kerjanya Lengkap
summary: Apa itu Teknik Informatika? Mengapa lulusan Teknik Informatika sangat dibutuhkan saat ini? Simak selengkapnya di sini!
body_text: Daftar isi Di era modern yang semuanya serba digital seperti sekarang ini, membuat Information Technology (IT) sudah menjadi kebutuhan utama. Hal ini dikarenakan di berbagai aspek kehidupan manusia membutuhkan teknologi untuk membantu berbagai aktivitas sehari-hari. Akibat dari perkembangan teknologi yang pesat ini, membuat kebutuhan akan ahli di bidang informatika semakin dan akan terus meningkat. Maka dari itu, di sekolah menengah dan perguruan tinggi mengajarkan tentang informatika ataupun teknik informatika. Bila kamu termasuk salah satu orang yang tertarik untuk berkuliah di bidang ini, simak penjelasan selengkapnya mengenai jurusan teknik informatika hingga prospek kerjanya berikut. Apa itu informatika? Sebelum terjun membahas tentang jurusan teknik informatika, akan lebih baik untuk paham mengenai informatika terlebih dahulu. Informatika adalah suatu bidang ilmu yang berkaitan dengan teknologi dan pengolahan informasi. Informatika sendiri membahas studi, perancangan, pengolahan dan pembuatan sistem komputasi yang kemudian diproses dan disajikan sebagai informasi. Dalam bidang informatika, berbagai peralatan teknologi mulai dari komputer hingga gadget sudah dianggap sebagai sahabat. Meskipun begitu, keberadaan peralatan tersebut hanya sebagai sebuah media yang dapat digunakan sehingga para penggunanya bisa menerima dan mengolah berbagai informasi dan data. Fungsi informatika Seperti yang sudah dipaparkan sebelumnya, teknologi dibutuhkan di berbagai aspek kehidupan. Sehingga bisa dikatakan bahwa informatika sendiri berfungsi untuk menjembatani manusia untuk mendapatkan segala jenis informasi yang bisa didapat melalui teknologi. Selain itu, dengan adanya informatika, maka perkembangan dalam pembuatan suatu alat maupun aplikasi komputasi bisa terbantu. Kenapa informatika itu penting Setelah mengetahui fungsi informatika, akan muncul pertanyaan kenapa informatika itu penting? Adanya transisi yang kini menjadi era digital terjadi karena adanya inovasi dan perkembangan dari teknologi inovasi di berbagai bidang dalam kehidupan. Perkembangan teknologi yang terjadi ini tidak lain karena dampak dari kemajuan informatika. Penjelasan Jurusan Teknik Informatika Salah satu jurusan yang berperan penting dalam dunia IT adalah jurusan teknik informatika. Jurusan ini juga dikenal dengan ilmu programming . Jurusan teknik informatika adalah suatu bidang yang mempelajari cara menggunakan teknologi komputer sebaik mungkin sehingga dapat mengatasi segala jenis permasalahan maupun pengolahan data dan informasi secara logika. Bagi kamu yang tertarik dengan dunia teknologi, pemrograman, dan pengoperasian komputer, teknik informatika merupakan jurusan yang tepat di perkuliahan. Baca juga: informasi terbaru Penerimaan Mahasiswa Baru UNM 2022 Materi kuliah jurusan teknik informatika Jurusan Teknik informatika mempelajari teknologi komputer meliputi analisis matematis pengembangan, pengujian, evaluasi perangkat lunak ( software ), sistem operasi, dan kerja komputer. Secara khusus, mahasiswa jurusan teknik informatika akan mempelajari fungsi-fungsi dan struktur instruksi dalam bahasa pemrograman untuk diaplikasikan pada komputer. Bahasa pemrograman menggunakan algoritma dan coding sehingga membutuhkan ilmu dasar matematika dan logika yang kuat. Selain menerapkan teknologi yang sudah ada, mahasiswa jurusan teknik informatika juga dituntut berpikir kreatif untuk menciptakan ide baru pada sistem operasi komputer. Mata kuliah dalam jurusan teknik informatika akan fokus pada pemrograman, teknologi jaringan komputer, dan pengembangan perangkat lunak. Mata kuliah itu di antaranya sistem informasi, logika informatika, strategi algoritma, rekayasa perangkat lunak, Artificial Intelligence (AI), dan pemrograman Internet. Kuliah jurusan teknik informatika dapat diselesaikan dalam waktu normal empat tahun atau delapan semester. Lebih lanjut, lulusan ini diharapkan dapat menjadi ahli dalam sistem operasi, aplikasi, dan komputer sehingga dapat memastikan IT dan sistem operasi bekerja dengan baik sesuai arahan yang sudah diinput. Jika kamu sebagai lulusan jursan teknik informatika dan berkarir di bidang yang sama, maka gaji yang akan didapat di tahapan awal karirmu yaitu di kisaran mulai dari Rp 5 juta hingga Rp 7 juta. Ahli IT dibutuhkan oleh setiap perusahaan yang mengandalkan teknologi untuk beroperasi, baik perusahaan negeri, swasta, maupun multinasional di berbagai sektor industri. title: How To Stop Punting Upgrades
summary: how-to-stop-punting-upgrades
body_text: For fast-growing companies, major dependency upgrades oftentimes find themselves struggling to move from the parking lot to the roadmap. The main reason why this happens is that growing companies (correctly) focus on shipping new, customer-visible features over the remediation of accumulated tech debt. In our experience, we’ve found it helpful to put upgrades in the same context as new features, and talk to the organization about the benefits of upgrades for both employees and customers. Security Security is probably the “easiest sell” for any company that has a security team or compliance obligations, it can ill afford to be on an unsupported version of a core dependency. Looking historically at attacks that caused catastrophic damage like Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228), Drupalgeddon (CVE-2018-7600), and Ghostcat (CVE-2020-1938), the effects of these vulnerabilities lingered because many companies needed to perform major upgrades to patch them. You probably already know whether your software is EOL’d, but in case you don’t check out a tool like endoflife.date . Performance Updates often include performance optimizations that can significantly enhance the efficiency of your application. These optimizations could mean faster response times, reduced resource consumption, and a more seamless user experience. If your company is focused on application performance metrics, you’ll want to look at the changelogs for your core dependencies and see if an upgrade gets you access to these improvements. For example, Python 3.12.0 brought performance improvements such as PEP 709 and the BOLT binary optimizer, which delivered an estimated 5% performance boost to upgraded applications. Ruby 3.3.0 brought the YJIT compiler, and optimizations in garbage collection and thread management​​​​, which boosted application performance up to 10%. Developer Experience If your company is making a big push on hiring engineers, you should make it clear that talented engineers don’t want to be working with unsupported versions of core frameworks. Not only is this a bad signal for the organization's commitment to great developer experience, it also can also contribute a ton of friction to general engineering velocity. Newer versions of packages are generally easier to maintain and extend, and allow development teams to leverage the latest features and paradigms. They’re also generally more feature-rich, increasing the number of building blocks available to your team for new features. Final Thoughts In isolation, the impact of skipping a few updates seems negligible, but the cumulative opportunity cost of not upgrading should be evaluated in the same category as major product features with associated revenue opportunities. Additionally, engineering teams should consider that the effort associated with most individual upgrades increases at an accelerating rate, which makes upgrades even more important to prioritize sooner rather than later. We’ll blog about this aspect of upgrade effort soon(er rather than later). If you need help prioritizing a major upgrade or scoping one to ensure it's done safely, contact us and we’ll advise- free of charge.

From the desks of Jonathan Cox, Jennifer Dooly and James Janoskey: Why permitting reform matters now
body_text: From the desks of Jonathan Cox, Jennifer Dooly and James Janoskey: Why permitting reform matters now By: Jonathan Cox, Jennifer Dooly and James Janoskey, Co-Heads of J.P. Morgan Investment Banking’s Natural Resources Group July 09, 2026 SHARE LINKEDIN FACEBOOK COPYLINK EMAIL PRINT We spend our days advising the companies building the physical backbone of the global economy—energy producers, power developers, miners, midstream operators, manufacturers, and infrastructure sponsors. One issue comes up more consistently than any other, and it isn't access to capital: it's permitting. The concern is not confined to one region or political camp. We hear it from sponsors and investors, utilities and system operators, labor and local leaders, landowners, community groups, and public agencies. What we see Across sectors, the biggest issue is whether projects can reach a final, durable decision on a schedule that investors, communities, and supply chains can plan around. Grid connection queues in the UK and Germany can now stretch a decade or more, and major project timelines in Canada and Australia have lengthened materially over the past five years. New generation and storage projects are routinely delayed by reviews, interconnection studies, and sequencing across agencies, meaning capacity that could be built is stuck in process even when capital and technology are ready. The constraint is most acute in the United States, where shifting permitting requirements across jurisdictions compounds costs, erodes stakeholder support, and can stall otherwise viable projects. A new report from the National Association of Manufacturers puts the annual cost to U.S. manufacturers at $7.9 billion in lost revenue, legal expenses, and delayed project initiation. McKinsey estimates that major U.S. projects now take 4–5 years to permit, holding up roughly $1.1–$1.5 trillion in infrastructure investment. These figures represent generation capacity not coming online, grid upgrades not being delivered, and industrial facilities not being built. All of these inefficiencies show up as higher costs, tighter supply, and reduced resilience when needs are skyrocketing. Our view The case for permitting reform in the U.S. is about modernization, not deregulation: predictable timelines, durable decisions, and less duplication – while preserving appropriate safety standards, environmental safeguards, and community benefits. When the process itself becomes the primary source of risk, that uncertainty shows up in financing terms, hurdle rates, and final investment decisions, sometimes tipping the balance toward projects abroad. There is also growing demand for broad, durable bipartisan legislation that can support a wide range of permitted projects and that can outlast election cycles, so multi-year projects aren’t forced to reprice, redesign, or restart. Capital formation and long-term societal planning both depend on rules stable enough for multi-year investments, community benefit negotiations, workforce development, and supply-chain buildout to hold together. “ The connection is clear: when permitting works, capital moves quickly into productive assets. When it doesn't, projects stall, costs rise, and the United States cedes ground in industries where leadership is not optional. Jonathan Cox, Jennifer Dooly and James Janoskey Our stake JPMorganChase finances and advises clients building tangible infrastructure and industry worldwide such as grid upgrades, domestic manufacturing, critical minerals, semiconductors, and energy infrastructure. The firm's Security and Resiliency Initiative reflects a particular focus on the United States: a $1.5 trillion, 10-year plan including an initial $10 billion in direct equity investments in U.S.-based companies strengthening energy independence, advanced manufacturing, and infrastructure. The connection is clear: when permitting works, capital moves quickly into productive assets. When it doesn't, projects stall, costs rise, and the United States cedes ground in industries where leadership is not optional. Critical components for permitting reform in the U.S. First, permitting should be timely and predictable by design, including the use of enforceable schedules, concurrent rather than sequential reviews, and digital workflows. The European Commission's European Grids Package illustrates what this could look like at scale: harmonized deadlines (e.g., two years to grant permits for new transmission and distribution), a centralized national digital portal, and narrower reviews for upgrades or repowering where risk is well understood. Second, judicial review must remain a safeguard but deliver decisions on a timeline that matches economic reality. Today, even unsuccessful challenges add years and function as a financing premium on nationally important projects. Tighter statutes of limitation, accelerated judicial review, and standing limited to substantive participants could preserve accountability while reducing investment-deterring uncertainty, an idea with strong bipartisan support. Third, government coordination and capacity should be treated as core infrastructure. Several states have shown that creating a clearer ‘front door,’ with centralized coordination and defined accountability, can significantly reduce timeline risk without compromising standards. A recent Western Governors’ Association initiative points in this same direction, launching a Permitting Alignment and Coordination Task Force that aims to improve state and federal level coordination by creating a governor-led framework to align permitting processes, resolve interstate bottlenecks, and advance multi-state priority infrastructure projects more efficiently. The bottom line The United States can build faster without cutting corners. Our clients are ready to deploy capital into projects that expand capacity, lower costs, strengthen supply chains, and create jobs. Capital is global, and the window to secure America's share is narrower than it seems. We will keep supporting our clients and engaging constructively with policymakers to help deliver a permitting system that is modern, accountable, and built for the scale of what this country needs to accomplish.
